paragraphs: Safety
Laboratory and Safety Management
Our project has received institutional permission to conduct the required experiments. The laboratory operates at Biosafety Level 1 (BSL-1).

Our Principal Investigator and safety officer is Dr. Jian Mo, who holds a PhD in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology and has more than ten years of laboratory research and management experience. He has received biosafety training and certification in laboratory safety management. His responsibilities include overseeing safety procedures, member training, risk assessments, and compliance with laboratory standards.
Safety Training

Our safety introduction covers the distinction between biosafety and biosecurity, research risk assessment, Dual-Use Research of Concern (DURC), gain-of-function experiments, biological hazard classification, and laboratory containment levels.
Additional topics include personal protective equipment, biological waste disposal, emergency responses to spills and contamination, and the ethical and safety boundaries of genetic engineering.
Experimental Chassis and Gene Origin
Our project uses Escherichia coli DH5α as the experimental chassis and ISCro4 as the target of directed evolution, aiming to improve its efficiency in DNA excision, integration, and inversion.

Citrobacter rodentium, listed in our Responsible Research Form, is the source organism of ISCro4. We did not use or culture this source organism in our experiments. The BSL-2 designation in the form refers to the source organism itself and does not indicate that BSL-2 strains were used in this project.
Experimental work was conducted in a BSL-1 laboratory under GMO containment requirements, with no field trials or cultivation in open environments.
Laboratory Safety Facilities

The laboratory is equipped with an eyewash station, an emergency shower, Class II biosafety cabinets, and autoclaves. Additional facilities include fire extinguishers, spill kits, fume hoods, designated biohazard waste bins, and hand-washing sinks.
Personal protective equipment includes laboratory coats and goggles. Disinfectants are available at laboratory benches for routine surface disinfection.
Biological Material and Waste Management

Biosafety cabinets, sealed culture vessels, routine surface disinfection, personal protective equipment, and access restrictions are used to reduce the risk of unintended GMO release. Engineered strains are stored in locked, sealed containers, and transport outside the laboratory is restricted.

Solid waste contaminated with GMOs is collected in sealed biohazard bags and autoclaved. Liquid cultures undergo disinfectant treatment. Residual GMO materials are inactivated before leaving the laboratory.

Standard laboratory antibiotics are used in routine molecular cloning experiments. Antibiotic-containing media and waste are handled according to laboratory biosafety procedures to minimize risks associated with antibiotic resistance.
Access Control and Biosecurity

Laboratory access is controlled through facial recognition, allowing entry only to registered personnel. Visitors must apply in advance and be accompanied by laboratory personnel. Entry and exit records are automatically logged.

Traditional locks are also used, with keys distributed only to a limited number of authorized personnel. Our project focuses on developing tools for DNA manipulation, and the team's work in this project does not involve DURC-related issues.
Ethical Considerations
The project does not involve animal experiments or samples derived from animals or humans. No research involving human participants, including questionnaires or interviews, is planned.

The team's work in this project does not involve ethical issues arising from these activities. The project aims to develop tools for manipulating large DNA fragments, with potential benefits for biotechnology practitioners and, in the longer term, patients with genetic diseases.
